notes.meaning: Paul explains that boasting does no real good, but his rivals have forced him into it. He shifts attention away from his own deeds to visions and direct revelations given to him by the Lord.

Paul describes an event from fourteen years earlier when a believer—speaking humbly of himself—was taken up into the third heaven. He admits he does not know whether this happened physically in his body or outside it in spirit, because only God knows. The third heaven refers to the highest place of all, where God lives in majesty.

Paul repeats that only God knows whether he was in his body or out of it during this journey. He was taken up into Paradise, the peaceful home of the blessed, and heard sacred things that human words cannot express. He was not permitted to share what he heard, because those words were meant only to encourage him in his own trials.

Paul is willing to speak highly of the man who received such wonderful heavenly experiences. When it comes to his ordinary daily life, however, he chooses to boast only about his weaknesses. This keeps the focus on God rather than on human greatness.

If Paul did choose to boast about these experiences, he would not be acting like a fool, because everything he said would be completely true. Yet he holds back from saying more. He wants people to judge him only by the life they see him live and the message they hear him preach.

To stop Paul from becoming proud after receiving such great revelations, God allowed a sharp trial described as a thorn in his flesh. This painful trouble acted like an enemy messenger buffeting and beating him down. Even though Satan meant it for harm, God used it to protect Paul from conceit.

differ.view: The thorn is understood broadly as all kinds of outward trials, distresses, and temptations that afflict human weakness, rather than one specific bodily sickness.
The thorn is commonly viewed as a lasting physical affliction, like severe eye trouble, or the ongoing attacks of false teachers.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Many older Latin writers saw the thorn as painful temptations toward sexual sin, while some modern writers suggest it was an eye disease caused by the bright light on the road to Damascus.

notes.meaning: Paul went to the Lord three separate times to beg for this painful burden to be taken away. Just as Jesus prayed three times in the Garden of Gethsemane, Paul prayed persistently until the Lord gave him a clear answer.

The Lord replied that His grace—His freely given love, help, and favor—is all Paul needs. God's strength is shown most clearly when a person is weak and cannot rely on himself. Once Paul understood this, he gladly chose to boast in his physical limitations so that Christ's power would rest over him like a sheltering tent.

Paul learns to be well content with hardships, insults, lack of money, persecutions, and distresses when they happen for the sake of Christ. When he is drained of all human self-reliance, he receives divine strength to carry on. True spiritual power begins where human power ends.

Paul knows that praising himself looks foolish, but the Corinthians forced him into it by failing to defend his good name. They should have spoken up for him, because his service proved he was not behind their loud false teachers in any way, even though he knew he was nothing on his own.

Paul displayed the true marks of an apostle while living among the Corinthians, patiently bearing trouble while working miracles, wonders, and mighty deeds. These supernatural works were God's visible proof that Paul was a genuine messenger of Jesus.

differ.view: Miraculous signs were given specifically to the original apostles to establish the early church and ceased once the apostolic era came to an end.
Miracles were not limited only to apostles in the early church, and miraculous spiritual gifts continue in the church today.

notes.meaning: The Corinthian church received every spiritual benefit other churches received, with only one difference: Paul never asked them to pay for his living expenses. He playfully asks them to forgive him for this 'wrong' of serving them free of charge.

Paul is ready to visit Corinth a third time, and he still refuses to take any financial support from them. He does not want their money or belongings; he wants to help their souls. Just as loving parents save up to provide for their children rather than demanding support from them, Paul desires to provide for them as their spiritual father.
Paul is eager to spend everything he has and completely wear himself out to care for their souls. He will keep giving himself generously, even if they return his deep love with coldness.
Paul repeats a rumor invented by his enemies. These opponents admitted he did not take money in person, but they claimed he was secretly tricky and used others to get their money behind their backs.

differ.view: Paul is rejecting a dishonest rumor made against him, so this verse must never be used to justify trickery or deceit in doing religious work.

notes.meaning: Paul challenges the Corinthians to show if any worker he ever sent took financial advantage of them. Titus and the trusted Christian brother who traveled with him showed the exact same honest spirit and walked in the exact same upright steps as Paul.

Paul clarifies that he is not putting himself on trial before the Corinthians or merely making excuses for his behavior. He speaks honestly in the presence of God as a follower of Christ, and his true aim is to build up the believers in their faith.

Paul worries that his next visit might be painful if the believers have not turned away from their bad behavior. He fears he will find bitter fighting, envy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambition, slander, secret gossip, boastful pride, and confusion.

Paul fears that God will cause him deep sorrow and shame if he arrives and finds believers still caught in old sins. A faithful leader feels deep grief when church members refuse to repent of sexual wrongdoing and unclean living.
